extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers / students of creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance on composing short stories (including the short-short or conte) and on constructing novels, focusing on form, perspective, economy, openings, endings, and the match between subject and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of form (order of incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of form — defined as the order, in time and importance, in which the narrated incidents are grouped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form is the first condition of artistic expression; order incidents by temporal and importance priorities to create coherent structure. The author notes this is a classic/Latin tradition and that adherence clears the ground for good fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to appropriate form
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer must discern whether a subject is suited to the proportions of a short story or of a novel; if it appears adapted to both, it is probably inadequate to either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the subject requires gradual unfolding of inner life or the sense of lapse of time (novel) versus a concentrated situation (short story). Avoid forcing a subject into a format for which it is unsuited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time for short stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the old traditional unity of time — avoid marking a time-interval long enough to suggest modification in the characters or circumstances in a short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marking long time intervals will turn a short story into a compressed long tale or bald novel scenario; keep the short story temporally compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of vision / single pair of eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories should generally be seen through only one pair of eyes (unity of vision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the reflecting mind deliberately and stay within it; avoid attributing thoughts, metaphors, or knowledge to that mind which are not naturally within its register. This maintains probability and prevents incongruities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriately situated reflecting mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a narrator/witness whose mind is so situated and constituted as to take the widest possible view of the case you mean to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately choose and 'live inside' that mind — feel, see and react exactly as it would, no more and no otherwise — to avoid implausible reporting or attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain naturalness when handling improbability or the supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: When the effect sought is improbable (e.g., ghost stories), the more studied the approach must be and the more perfectly maintained the air of naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the reader an easy assumption that events are likely to happen in that way; avoid irrelevant touches or inattention that will undo the spell. Example: great ghost stories are models of subtle artifice; it's not enough to believe in ghosts — the historian's description must convince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish reader confidence immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief obligations in a short story is to give the reader an immediate sense of security: every phrase should be a sign-post, not a misleading one; the reader must feel that he can trust the author's guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once trust is gained, you may lead the reader into incredible adventures; if the reader loses faith in the author's sureness of foot, the tale's spell collapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the appearance of improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: Improbability itself is not a danger, but the appearance of improbability is — except in cases based on pathological conditions or culturally inherited beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accounts and descriptions make the improbable appear credible; avoid unconvinced or inconsistent reporting that exposes improbability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus and economy: avoid splintering the reader's attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid distracting and splintering the reader's attention; horrors or incidents, if multiplied, should be cumulative and not dispersed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fewer, cumulative elements are stronger: quiet iteration is more racking than diversified assaults. Keep attention tightened on the central nerve of the tale (example: 'The Turn of the Screw' sustains one dread throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain a single dominant dread or theme in horror
rubrics_metrics.description: In tales of horror the economy of horror should sustain one principal dread — no diversion from that one dread should be attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous expectation of the central threat (e.g., in 'The Turn of the Screw' the reader always expects to meet one of the two evil figures) intensifies fear; diversions weaken the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short story concerns situation; novel concerns character
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief technical difference: situation is the main concern of the short story, character the main concern of the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short stories depend on form and presentation to create vividness and presentness; novels require development of characters over time to keep a work 'alive.' Adjust priorities accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right angle / presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The short-story writer must know from what angle to present his anecdote so it will 'give out all its fires' and understand why that particular angle is the right one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the subject over, apply laws of perspective, and select the presentation that best reveals the subject in concentrated form; the chosen angle should make the anecdote feel natural and unembellished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize technical artifice; preserve only the surviving minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the technical trick to its minimum — the surviving minimum is the only bridge between the reader's imagination and the author's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like an actress using little paint, aim for the least visible craft that still secures the effect; over-embellishment breaks the illusion of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong opening / 'attack' with germ of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The short-story writer's first care should be to know how to make a beginning: the first page ought to contain the germ of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest attention with a vivid, telling opening (the 'salamander' anecdote). But ensure the opening is more than a trick — it must be justified by a living core that makes the attention worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening must be supported by a substantial core (the 'salamander')
rubrics_metrics.description: It is useless to box the reader's ear unless you have a salamander to show him — the attention-grabbing opening must rest on a living, moving substance that makes the story worth telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening should 'situate' the tale and serve as a clue to omitted detail; it must reflect deep familiarity with the subject rather than superficial flashy start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain firm grasp on subject and order essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Never forget what you want to tell or why it seems worth telling; intensity of hold on the subject presupposes prior thinking and the instinct of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter stories rely heavily on selection and the order in which essentials are set forth; be disciplined in what is kept and how it is sequenced to preserve momentum and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sketchiness — suggest fullness within narrow limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contenting oneself with a mere sketch; true achievement is to suggest illimitable air within a narrow space rather than provide a mere skeleton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be economical but not paring to the point of deprivation; some tales appear brief but are the result of adroit extraction of significance rather than omission of enriching dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrivance and gratuitous incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hunt about for arbitrary combinations of circumstance or fortuitous pretexts to manufacture climax or reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners often crowd accidental happenings and minor episodes into their work; instead let the subject grow slowly in the mind, and draw significance from internal logic rather than added effects (example: unnecessary runaway-horse episode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced economy and expenditure (pay the expense)
rubrics_metrics.description: True economy consists in drawing out of one's subject every drop of significance it can give; true expenditure consists in devoting time, meditation and patient labour to extraction and representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as an investment: do not confuse economy with parsimony nor expenditure with waste. The 'expense' of time and thought is necessary to produce concentrated, resonant fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate degree of character development
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories may rely more on type and situation (characters can be slightly less than fully individuated); novels require characters that are alive and capable of sustaining the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short stories, a few strokes can set a type effectively; for novels, allow space for the unfolding of personality and continuous growth over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending must be inevitable and true to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to end a tale in accordance with its own deepest sense deprives it of meaning; an inadequate or unreal ending diminishes value as much as in the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid standardized, machine-made endings; work toward a conclusion that feels inevitable (Nietzsche: genius to 'make an end'). The conclusion should grow naturally from the subject's own dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using long time-lapses in short fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more retarding than the marking of a time-interval long enough to suggest modification in the personages or their circumstances in a short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject requires suggestion of the lapse of time, it may be more suitable for the novel or the long short-story (intermediate form). Use time-lapse only when a single retrospective flash will suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the novel types and methods (mans, psychology, adventure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most novels group under manners, character (psychology), and adventure — each implies different methods and emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the novel's type consciously since method and treatment differ (e.g., 'Vanity Fair' for manners, 'Madame Bovary' for character). Recognize adventure-novel is the least modern; match form to tradition and aims.
